headline: Adrafinil keeps your Mac awake only while AI agents work
summary: This new macOS app prevents sleep, including clamshell mode, only when an AI coding agent is actively processing tasks.
details: Adrafinil is a new macOS menu bar application designed to intelligently manage your Mac's sleep behavior. Unlike traditional utilities that force your machine to stay awake indefinitely, Adrafinil intervenes only when an AI coding agent, such as Claude Code or Cursor, has an active session. Once the agent completes its task, the Mac returns to its normal sleep state.

The app offers a sophisticated alternative to always-on wake utilities. It monitors AI agent activity and blocks sleep, even when the lid is closed (clamshell mode), exclusively during active processing. When no agent is working, closing the lid will put the Mac to sleep as usual, conserving power and ensuring the machine rests when not in use.

Overriding system sleep, especially in clamshell mode, requires privileged access. Adrafinil handles this by isolating the core sleep-blocking functionality in a small, audited helper application. This helper exposes a minimal interface, with all policy managed by an unprivileged daemon, ensuring security and control.

Adrafinil utilizes standard macOS power management assertions for idle sleep and `pmset disablesleep` for clamshell sleep. It ensures that the Mac is only kept awake when necessary, preventing the displayless, lid-closed machine from staying awake unnecessarily.

The application is distributed as a signed and notarized disk image, requiring macOS 10.14 or later. Upon first launch, it requests administrator rights to register the privileged helper. Developers can also build and test Adrafinil directly from its Xcode project, with components authorized by the developer's own signing team.

The name 'Adrafinil' is a nod to the eugeroic drug of the same name, reflecting the app's purpose: to promote wakefulness only when there is work to be done. It's developed by @kageroumado and available at kagerou.glass.

headline_marked: [[GLP-1 drugs]] reverse depression-like behavior in mice, study finds
headline: GLP-1 drugs reverse depression-like behavior in mice, study finds
summary: Researchers discovered that GLP-1 drugs, known for weight loss, may also act as antidepressants by promoting beneficial gut bacteria growth.
details: Ozempic and other GLP-1 drugs, primarily used for weight loss, have shown an unexpected bonus: alleviating symptoms of depression in some patients. A new study from Southeast University in China suggests a mechanism involving the gut microbiome.

Researchers observed that individuals with major depressive disorder often have lower natural levels of GLP-1. When tested on mice, GLP-1 drugs not only induced weight loss but also reversed depression-like behaviors, indicating a potential antidepressant effect.

Blocking the GLP-1 receptor in mice affected weight loss but not the reversal of depression, suggesting the antidepressant effect is independent of weight management. Crucially, in germ-free mice, the antidepressant effect was absent, highlighting the role of gut microbes.

The study found that GLP-1 drugs promote the growth of Lactobacillus delbrueckii, a bacterium that produces endocannabinoids. These compounds help reduce stress responses in the brain, acting as natural mood boosters.

To confirm causality, researchers transferred fecal matter from GLP-1-treated mice to depressed mice, which resulted in improved mood. Similarly, directly administering L. delbrueckii to depressed mice also had an antidepressant effect, identifying it as a 'psychobiotic'.

While L. delbrueckii is known for its presence in fermented foods like yogurt and kefir, it's important to note its potential to act as a pathogen in other contexts. The study also found that different GLP-1 drugs had varying impacts on the gut microbiome.
